newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnian Serb leader detained in power struggle.
newsitem.headline: Bosnian Serb leader detained in power struggle.

text.p: Bosnian Serb President Biljana Plavsic on Monday accused hardliners of trying to oust her and said indicted war criminal Radovan Karadzic was still running the government.

She spoke to independent Belgrade radio station B-92 after Serb sources said she was detained overnight by government opponents trying to sabotage her attempts to crackdown on high level corruption in the Bosnian Serb republic.

Plavsic did not confirm she was held against her will but NATO peacekeepers gave her an escort to leave the northeastern town of Bijeljina where she spent the night meeting party and military officials at a hotel heavily guarded by police.
Asked by B-92 if she thought she was the victim of a coup, she said: "Yes, I do."
Plavsic said she was preparing a report which would show "who is actually running the Bosnian Serb republic" and identified Karadzic who was "telling people to obstruct state institutions."
She replaced Karadzic as president last year when the international community forced him from public office for his conduct of the 1992-95 Bosnian war.
Karadzic has continued to wield political and economic influence from behind the scenes in collaboration with Momcilo Krajisnik, the Serb member of Bosnia's multi-ethnic collective presidency.

Plavsic told B-92 she did not want either NATO peacekeepers or the Bosnian Serb army to intervene in her conflict with the hardliners which became public when she failed at the weekend to secure the dismissal of Interior Minister Dragan Kijac.
She accused Kijac, a Karadzic loyalist, of refusing to investigate two large Bosnian Serb companies associated with former president and Krajisnik.
Plavsic went from Bilejina to her headquarters at Banja Luka in north Bosnia while hardliners met in their Pale stronghold outside Sarajevo to discuss her future.
Western diplomats, who see Plavsic as more pragmatic than Karadzic loyalists, were concerned over the political turmoil but said they had "limited options".
Mediators were keen to avoid a repeat of last year's failed attempt by international High Representative Carl Bildt to promote a rival challenging Karadzic's allies.

Bildt suffered a humiliating defeat when he openly supported former prime minister Rajko Kasagic in a power struggle with Karadzic's party. Kasagic was removed and branded a traitor plotting with foreign envoys.

Major powers were particularly concerned about the effect of the conflict on plans to hold local elections in September. If Plavsic were stripped of authority, agreements on election rules could be jeopardised, diplomats said.
With Karadzic and Krajisnik retaining control over the ruling party and the police, Plavsic has few tools at her disposal.
But despite her weak position, she has refused to back down and local media alleged she possessed damaging documents about monopolies run by Karadzic and Krajisnik.

"She must have worked out how is she going to play this. The fact that she's got all this information that could discredit Krajisnik and Karadzic is rather like an insurance policy," one diplomat, who asked not to be named, told Reuters.
Plavsic was elected president of the Bosnia's Serb entity last September in a vote which put post-war government structures in place under the Dayton peace agreement.
